title: Asymmetric Egress Control and mTLS Adaptation Notes
body:
Context and motivation:

We continue to see complexity when a single client-facing path traverses multiple control-plane domains (regional control planes, dedicated pools, and 3rd-party edge partners). Past solutions focused on symmetric policy (same set of checks both ingress and egress), but in practice we need asymmetric handling for performance and compatibility: short, permissive egress to critical external caches or legacy partners, and strict mTLS for intra-cluster/service-mesh hops. This doc captures notes and proposals for an asymmetric egress control pattern and how to adapt mTLS semantics when traffic crosses control-plane boundaries.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Clear rules for when to require end-to-end mTLS vs. when to allow mTLS termination/fallback at a boundary.
- Fallback behavior that preserves availability while minimizing blast radius (observability & rollback hooks).
- Simple, auditable control-plane API for declaring egress exceptions per route (with scope: region/namespace/customer).
- Backward-compatible handling for legacy partners that cannot do mTLS but must be reachable at low latency.

Terminology:
- Ingress boundary: external edge (API gateway / CDN front) where client TLS terminates.
- Control-plane boundary: change in authority (e.g., us-west control plane -> eu-west control plane, or hosted->dedicated).
- Egress sandbox: the first hop out of our mesh (eg. to a 3rd-party cache, partner API, or cloud firewall).
- Policy scope: route-level, service-level, or tenant-level.

Current problems observed:
1) Unannounced control-plane handoffs cause mTLS handshake failures for long-lived connections (KV cache reuse relies on same cert pool).
2) Broad egress allowlists reduce security; narrow allowlists cause high operational cost and fragile failovers.
3) Service mesh sidecars assume uniform identity model; cross-region routing sometimes rewrites headers in ways that break identity validation.
4) Observability: egress decisions lack token-level signal; hard to attribute which policy caused fallback.

Proposed asymmetric egress pattern (high-level):
1) Classify egress destinations into three tiers:
   - Tier A: internal services (same mesh/identity domain) -> require mutual TLS, full identity propagation, strict mTLS validation.
   - Tier B: trusted external partners (regional partners, partner caches) -> prefer mTLS where supported; allow short-lived TLS or authenticated HTTPS as fallback.
   - Tier C: public/unknown endpoints (third-party APIs) -> standard TLS with egress least-privilege network controls and per-route rate/timeout policies.

2) At control-plane boundaries, apply an explicit "identity translation" operation rather than implicit termination:
   - If Tier A traffic crosses boundary, attempt to preserve identity via federated trust (exchange or map certs), otherwise fail closed with configurable soft-fail windows.
   - For Tier B, allow certificate translation: the outgoing control plane may re-issue a short-lived client cert representing the original service (auditing metadata attached).
   - For Tier C, terminate mesh mTLS at boundary and use a gateway-to-external TLS connection; log identity and route metadata for audit.

3) Policy surface (control-plane API) must include:
   - scope (region, project, namespace, customer)
   - destination classification (A/B/C) and allowed fallback levels
   - max soft-fail window (duration), and circuit-break configuration for failures
   - audit slab id and owner (who owns this exception)

mTLS adaptation techniques (options with tradeoffs):
- Federated root pools: Share root CA sets across control planes. Pros: preserves end-to-end mTLS. Cons: CA sprawl; revocation complexity.
- Short-lived translation certs: Boundary control plane issues short-lived certs and includes signed metadata linking back to original identity. Pros: flexible; easier revocation. Cons: trust model needs explicit acceptance by endpoints.
- SPIFFE/SPIRE identity mapping: Use SPIFFE IDs and let each control plane assert spiffe://... identities with a translation registry. Pros: standards-based. Cons: requires SPIs across all partners.
- Application-level attestation header: For partners that cannot validate certs, include an attestation header with signed claim that downstream can opt to trust. Pros: low client change. Cons: less cryptographic assurance; must guard header injection.

Observability and audit requirements:
- Every boundary translation must create an immutable event with: original identity, translated identity, translation reason, timestamp, boundary id, policy id.
- Expose metrics: translation_count, translation_failure_rate, fallback_count_by_route, avg_handshake_latency_by-tier.
- Correlate egress exceptions to consumer tokens/route ids for cost attribution.

Fallback and gradual rollout strategy:
1) Start with a "monitoring-only" mode for new translation rules: allow translation but force logs + alerts when translation occurs.
2) Soft-fail: treat translation failures as warning for T seconds, then enforce fail-closed for T2 seconds (configurable per-policy).
3) Canary rollouts by region and by tenant. Use traffic mirroring to test translated path behavior without affecting production.

Control-plane design implications:
- Policy datastore needs multi-region reconciliation and strong consistency for critical rules; we should prefer leader region for writes with cached reads and TTL-based local fallbacks.
- Identities & keys: central KMS for signing translation tokens with per-region signing proxies. Key rotation must be coordinated across regions to prevent transient trust breakage.
- Rollback hooks: any policy push must support immediate revert and an automated fallback route to known-good translation behavior.

Service mesh interactions and required changes:
- Sidecars should expose an outbound egress classifier that consults local policy and can call a region-local control plane to determine translation actions. Keep sidecar decision lightweight (cache decisions).
- Gateways should be able to attach signed translation metadata (not just opaque headers) and reject requests lacking provenance if policy requires.
- Avoid header-only origin proofs unless wrapped by signed tokens to prevent header spoofing by inside attackers.

Operational runbook (initial):
- Day 0: Define Tier mappings for top 50 routes (owner + justification).
- Day 1: Deploy translation audit events and metrics collector to staging. Configure the initial set of rules in monitor-only mode for 48–72 hours.
- Day 3: Review alerts and decide per-route whether to enable soft-fail or fail-closed.
- Week 2: Expand to 75% of important routes, start regional canaries for EU/US handoffs.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Which partner endpoints will accept translation certs? Need outreach and a compatibility matrix. (Action: Lina to own partner outreach; due 2025-02-14)
- How to model revocation for translated certs? (Tech debt spike: evaluate SPIRE vs. short-lived certs)
- Cost model: how much extra latency do translations add under peak? Need perf runs (JIRA-ENG-4999).
- Does our compliance posture (SOC2) require us to avoid header-based attestations for certain tenants? (Security to confirm)

References and quick links:
- RFC: internal egress policy proto (github.com/redwood-inference/routing-protos/blob/main/egress_policy.md)
- Confluence: Egress Control Playbook (linked_artifacts above)
- Ticket: JIRA-ENG-4872 (region handoff incident)

Appendix: sample policy YAML (human-readable snippet)

policy_id: translate-cache-to-partner-01
scope: project:search-service, region:us-west
destination: partner-cache.example.com
classification: TierB
fallback: tls-https
translation: short-lived-cert
soft_fail_window_seconds: 30
audit_owner: @search-platform

Notes: This snippet is intentionally simplified. Real policy will include allowed ciphers, subject constraints, and ratelimits.

End of notes.

Action items (owners):
- Lina: compile partner capability matrix (due 2025-02-14)
- Marco: prototype short-lived translation cert proxy (POC by 2025-03-01)
- Tom: add translation telemetry to tracing pipeline and create dashboard (target 2025-02-28)

If you don’t hear otherwise, I’ll start the staging monitor-only rollout next week and open JIRA tickets for each route we change. Feedback welcome — especially on trust model preferences (federated-root vs. translation cert).
